#3162. 3 Things Dario Amodei Wants You To Know About Anthropic

Amodei had a chance to speak directly to investors at the IPO on Thursday.

By Jeremy Bowman – Nov 20, 2026 at 4:05PM EST

10 stocks we like better than Anthropic ›

It seems fitting in some ways that Anthropic's (ANT -8.50%) IPO came just a week after Nvidia's Jensen Huang resigned as CEO, leaving the chipmaker in turmoil. Nvidia had been the stock market's avatar for AI since the launch of ChatGPT, but with Anthropic now becoming the first AI lab to go public, it's set to take over as the market's best reflection of AI sentiment.

Anthropic is a pure-play AI company founded in 2021 by a group of former OpenAI employees who thought that company was too weak on safety. Anthropic builds AI models and software products based on its frontier intelligence platform, Claude.

Anthropic's IPO also gave the company a chance to have the investing world's full attention, and CEO Dario Amodei spoke for about five minutes at the Nasdaq stock exchange Thursday, sharing his vision for the company. Here are three things investors should know about the newly public company, direct from Amodei.

Dario Amodei. Image source: Getty Images.

Anthropic has made its prioritization of safety clear from its inception, and AI safety has only become more salient amid concerns of AI models going rogue, escaping sandboxes, and the intensifying competition with China.

Anthropic's emphasis on safety may also be a competitive advantage at a time when AI is facing a backlash. The midterm elections reflected growing discontent with data centers and could lead to a slowdown or increased restrictions on them, at least in some states.

The emphasis on safety also acts in the company's interest in terms of liability and reputational damage, as the future of AI is wide open and will be determined by companies like Anthropic.

Amodei told the audience, "There's a gigantic difference between how AI will go if we pay little attention to safety versus how it will go if we are obsessed with safety, and an obsession with safety and public benefit has been built into Anthropic's DNA from the start."

Amodei wants everyone, including investors, users, and AI skeptics, to know that he's one of the good guys.

In a similar vein, Amodei described a best-case scenario for the AI competition as a "race to the top."

Amodei said, "If we can show it's possible to make the right choices on safety and still build an incredibly successful company, others will be inspired to do the same."

If that spirit takes hold in the industry, then, he said, everybody wins, no matter who has the best models. Amodei assured investors that they intend to lead that race, saying, "The race to the top works best when driven from the front of the pack, and we fully hope and expect to do so, but the goal is to make the whole industry better, regardless of whether Anthropic is winning or losing at any given time."

Amodei began his comments with a story about how his father died of a disease, Hepatitis C, that was cured just a few years later.

The event clearly showed Amodei the power of invention and new technology, and after beginning his career in biology, he moved over to artificial intelligence, where he sees the potential for tremendous breakthroughs in medicine and beyond.

The departure of Jensen Huang due to a scandal involving multiple affairs is a reminder of the importance of character in leadership, and Amodei seems to possess that sufficiently.

Anthropic is a mission-driven company and the rare public benefit corporation on the stock market. Amodei brings a deep commitment to that mission and a personal passion for research and intelligence that can cure diseases and solve humanity's most pressing problems.

That's good news for Anthropic investors and should reassure them at a time when the AI trade looks more wobbly than ever.

#3161. How Often Do You Need To Scrub The Do Not Call List? The 31-Day Rule Explained

Phil Portman is a serial entrepreneur and the Founder & CEO of Textdrip — a small business SMS marketing tool to automate SMS campaigns.

​I see businesses repeatedly making the same mistake: They scrub their contact list once and then keep calling and texting from that list for months. That’s a risky habit, because every day new numbers join the Do Not Call Registry. A list that was clean in January can be full of problems by March.

After years of experience working in a regulated industry, I’m sure about one thing: Businesses rarely fail because the rules are unclear. They fail because their processes break down in practice. The Do Not Call rules are a crystal-clear example of this.

How often do you have to scrub the Do Not Call (DNC) list? Every 31 days. To keep safe harbor protection, you need to scrub against a version of the registry that is no more than 31 days old. In practice, that means every month.

The National Do Not Call Registry is run by the Federal Trade Commission (FTC). It lets people add their personal phone numbers to a list that tells telemarketers to stop contacting them. It exists to protect consumers who don’t want sales calls. It covers personal numbers, such as home and mobile lines. It doesn’t cover business-to-business calls to a company line. Knowing this difference helps you decide which numbers need a check.

Many teams assume it only covers voice calls, but it doesn’t. The Federal Communications Commission (FCC) treats text messages as calls, so the same protections apply to SMS marketing. If you text prospects, those numbers also need a DNC check.

State lists exist as well. Some states keep their own Do Not Call lists, and some, such as Florida and Texas, have stricter rules than the federal registry. If you contact people in several states, you need to check each state’s rules before you launch.

Some calls are exempt, such as those to people who gave written permission or have an established business relationship with you. Even then, you must honor opt-out requests.

To qualify for safe harbor under FTC and FCC regulations, telemarketers must scrub their list against the National DNC Registry. Every call must be made using a registry version downloaded no more than 31 days earlier. Simply put, you must rescrub every month. If it’s day 32, you’re already at risk.

Suppose you scrubbed a list on the first of the month. On the 20th, a prospect joins the registry. Your team keeps working that same list. Any call made after day 31 relies on an outdated version. Many teams scrub only when they upload new leads. This sounds fine, but a campaign can run for weeks, and a number can join the registry halfway through. If you keep contacting that number, you’re working from outdated data.

Safe harbor is a defense that protects a business when a call goes out by mistake. But it only applies if you had a working process in place before the mistake happened. A written policy that nobody reads or follows won’t help. Training without a current list won’t help either.

The FCC rule lists what a DNC safe harbor process needs:

• An internal Do Not Call list that is kept up to date.

• Registry access used to scrub within the 31-day window.

• Logs (records) showing when each scrub happened.

Record-keeping is a common gap. Without records, you have no safe harbor, even if the scrub did happen. If a regulator or a lawyer asks for proof, saying “we did it” won’t be enough. You need proof (dates and logs).

Do Not Call violations get expensive quickly. Under the Telephone Consumer Protection Act (TCPA), a consumer can sue for $500 per violation. If the violation was willful or knowing, a court can raise that to $1,500 per violation. A consumer generally must receive more than one call from the same business within 12 months to bring a DNC claim.

Some of these claims are filed as class actions. One outdated list can hold thousands of people, and each one may have a claim. A small gap in your process can turn into a very large bill. Legal fees and settlements add to that, along with damage to your business reputation.

I lead a company in a regulated industry, so I think about this often. Compliance works best when it is practiced as a routine instead of an event. We built Landline Remover to help teams make scrubbing a routine.

1. Scrub every time you upload leads, not just on launch day.

2. Rescrub active lists monthly, ideally a few days before the 31-day window closes.

3. Check your internal list and the national list together. Your internal do-not-call list holds people who told you directly to stop. The registry doesn’t know about them. Both lists matter.

4. Check reassigned numbers. Numbers change owners. The FCC’s reassigned numbers database can tell you whether a number has changed hands since you got consent.

5. Log every scrub with the date. That log is your proof if a court or regulator asks.

6. Automate the scrubbing process so it doesn’t depend on memory.

Do Not Call compliance is a monthly habit, not a one-time task. The rule is simple: scrub within 31 days, every time.

DNC scrubbing alone can’t protect a business. You need to keep proof that you followed the rule. Scrubbing only protects you if you can prove it. So build a regular scrubbing habit and keep the records. Remember that regulators don’t just look at your efforts—they ask for evidence.

#3160. Asked on Reddit: I Lost My Job; What Should I Do First?

We believe everyone should be able to make financial decisions with confidence. While we don't cover every company or financial product on the market, we work hard to share a wide range of offers and objective editorial perspectives.

So how do we make money? Our partners compensate us for advertisements that appear on our site. This compensation helps us provide tools and services - like free credit score access and monitoring. With the exception of mortgage, home equity and other home-lending products or services, partner compensation is one of several factors that may affect which products we highlight and where they appear on our site. Other factors include your credit profile, product availability and proprietary website methodologies.

However, these factors do not influence our editors' opinions or ratings, which are based on independent research and analysis. Our partners cannot pay us to guarantee favorable reviews. Here is a list of our partners.

Income loss is stressful; the first steps involve cutting costs and focusing on essentials.

A Redditor recently shared that they were struggling to decide which financial steps to take first after a job loss.

Should they withdraw money from retirement savings to have more cash on hand — but pay an early withdrawal penalty? Or is it better to rely on the severance payout to handle expenses?

Many users responded with good ideas: File for unemployment, try to avoid tapping into retirement savings, and cut expenses as much as possible.

For more ideas, I asked three financial experts how to manage money in the immediate aftermath of job loss.

While it’s tempting to make quick decisions about tapping into a retirement fund or selling a house, it’s better to wait on any big moves, says Parker Wine, retirement planning advisor at the financial firm Daniel A. White & Associates in Lewes, Delaware.

That’s because you need time to digest the situation and weigh the pros and cons of different options, he says. “People can get impulsive and panic, and it’s usually a bad thing to make decisions when you’re panicking,” he says.

Take your time, get second opinions and think through all of your options first, Wine suggests.

If you’re fortunate enough to receive a severance package, wait to sign it until you’ve reviewed it carefully and understand all of the details, says John Rafferty, partner and investment advisor representative at Solomon Financial in Carmel, Indiana.

For example, make sure you know about your health insurance options, such as whether you’ll receive insurance through COBRA or need to take out a new policy in the health insurance marketplace.

Filing for unemployment and checking into any other available workplace benefits — such as help with your new job search — is also an important part of understanding what support to expect in the weeks and months ahead, Rafferty adds.

Creating a bare-bones budget stripped of “extras” like restaurant meals or travel can help the severance payment last as long as possible, Rafferty says.

“Now that you don’t have income coming in, ask yourself, ‘How much can I spend and where?’”

You might be able to cut back on entertainment costs, coffee runs and clothing purchases, for example.

At the same time, it’s important to prioritize the essentials like mortgage payments, rent, utilities and food. Rafferty recommends calling your mortgage company, utilities provider and any other lenders to ask if they have a hardship program for those experiencing financial challenges.

Opting in could give you more time to pay your bills or temporarily lower payments.

It’s hard to stick to a budget that eliminates all entertainment, so Rafferty suggests finding enjoyable activities that come with a low price tag. Hiking, discovering a new park and participating in free community events are all ways to enjoy downtime on a budget.

“Having that release is mentally a big thing so you can stay prepared for the job search,” he says. “Otherwise, it’s easy to get down and feel negative, and we need things to help us feel positive.”

Similarly, connecting with friends and family during this time is crucial, says Laura Adams, accredited financial counselor and financial coach in Wilmington, North Carolina.

People often feel a sense of shame or embarrassment after job loss, and Adams encourages people to talk about their feelings and ask for help if needed. “Financial shame can cause us to make emotional rather than confident financial decisions,” she says.

Starting some kind of side hustle to bring in extra cash can also help bridge the gap between the job loss and your next job, Wine says. Substitute teaching, working at a local public golf course and driving for a rideshare service are all options he’s seen people try.

Doing something new also helps stave off boredom while unemployed, but he cautions that you’ll still owe taxes on any side income you bring in, so plan accordingly.

All three financial experts also emphasized that a job loss is easier to handle with an emergency savings fund you can turn to, and suggested building one up — ideally three to six months’ worth of expenses. But starting small helps, too — while employed, if possible.

The Redditor who posted the question mentioned that, like many Americans, they lacked emergency savings. This added urgency to the question of what to prioritize.

Reddit is an online forum where users share their thoughts in “threads” on various topics. The popular site includes plenty of discussion on financial subjects like how to deal with job loss, so we sifted through Reddit forums to get a pulse check. People post anonymously, so we cannot confirm their individual experiences or circumstances.

#3159. Top Wall Street analysts are bullish on the growth potential of these 3 stocks

Fears around the artificial intelligence trade and higher pressure on oil prices are weighing on global markets, but a few stocks offer investors solid growth prospects even in choppy times.

Investors with a long-term horizon can look beyond the ongoing volatility and track the recommendations of top Wall Street analysts to pick attractive stocks with strong long-term growth potential.

Here are three stocks favored by some of Wall Street's top pros, according to TipRanks, a platform that ranks analysts based on their past performance.

Health insurer UnitedHealth delivered better-than-expected results for the third quarter of 2026. The company also raised its full-year earnings outlook, reflecting continued progress on its turnaround plan.

Following the Q3 print, Morgan Stanley analyst Erin Wright reiterated a buy rating on UNH stock with a price target of $529. "UNH's beat & raise reinforces turnaround momentum, with improving MA [Medicare Advantage]/Optum Health supporting a higher '26 EPS baseline & upside to '27 consensus," said Wright.

The five-star analyst added that better-than-expected performance in the UnitedHealthcare and Optum Health businesses supported another upgrade to the company's 2026 adjusted earnings per share outlook to at least $20.50. Wright noted that UNH raised the earnings guidance despite incremental investments planned for the fourth quarter of 2026.

Furthermore, Wright highlighted management's view that the consensus 2027 EPS of $22.63 was too conservative. Reaching even the low end of the company's 13% to 16% long-term EPS growth target would imply an EPS of $23.17.

Wright raised her 2026 EPS estimate to $20.65 from $19.82 and 2027 EPS to $23.24 from $22.54, reflecting the latest upside and an improving 2026 medical loss ratio to 87.4% from 88.1%. Wright ranks No. 264 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. Her ratings have been successful 64% of the time, delivering an average return of 15%. See UnitedHealth Ownership Structure on TipRanks.

Social media giant Meta Platforms has been making headlines since the launch of its Muse AI agent, which is seeing solid traction. Investors look forward to updates on the company's AI strategy when it announces its third-quarter results on Oct. 21.

Heading into Q3 earnings, Guggenheim analyst Michael Morris maintained a buy rating on Meta stock and increased his price target to $850 from $700, reflecting higher estimates for 2027. He expects Muse usage momentum and engagement levels to shape investor sentiment into the Q3 earnings call.

Specifically, Morris highlighted that, according to Apptopia, Muse reached 1.3 million daily active users in five weeks versus 300,000 in the first week. Given that Muse's current adoption represents less than 0.05% of Meta's 3.6 billion daily active user base, the analyst expects management to prioritize boosting usage over near-term monetization.

"Over time, we believe Muse monetizes primarily through businesses paying to reach consumers through their agents, consistent with the economics of Meta's core advertising business, rather than consumer wallets," said the five-star analyst. He added that the checkout integrations with Shopify and PayPal reflect this framework.

While there are concerns that a rival could overtake Muse or the recently launched Muse Wonder and push Meta into a prolonged cycle of overinvestment, Morris remains bullish due to the company's strong record in scaling WhatsApp and competing strongly with TikTok via Reels as well as free distribution to an extensive user base.

Next is semiconductor company Marvell Technology. Earlier this month, Marvell held its Investor Day, where it raised its total addressable market estimate to $400 billion by 2030, reflecting solid AI-led demand tailwinds.

After hosting a non-deal roadshow with Marvell's senior management following the Investor Day, Stifel analyst Tore Svanberg reiterated a buy rating on the stock with a price target of $370.

The five-star analyst said that a major focus of the roadshow was the XPU and XPU Attach mix, as Marvell's Custom business expands toward its FY31 revenue target of $30 billion. In this regard, management reiterated that it expects a balanced mix of XPU and XPU Attach revenue in FY31, though it noted that either segment could grow rapidly enough to shift the mix toward 60/40 or 40/60.

While XPU drove most of the nearly $1.5 billion Custom revenue in FY26, Svanberg expects Marvell's XPU Attach business to grow substantially through the end of the decade, leading to a more balanced mix in this business. At the Investor Day event, the company raised its FY29 Custom target from more than $10 billion to over $12 billion, mainly driven by strength in the XPU Attach business.

Svanberg said that another key topic in the roadshow was whether Marvell can secure enough capacity to meet its raised targets. #3158. Colgate-Palmolive vs. lululemon athletica: Which Consumer Goods Stock Is a Better Buy for 2027?

Colgate-Palmolive's steady global staples business goes head-to-head with lululemon's premium apparel brand, and the valuation gap may surprise you.

By Sara Appino – Updated Nov 20, 2026 at 4:05PM EST

10 stocks we like better than Colgate-Palmolive ›

Choosing between a steady staples giant and a premium apparel leader requires balancing reliability against growth potential. Investors must decide if Colgate-Palmolive (CL +1.89%) or lululemon athletica (LULU -2.76%) better suits their 2027 goals.

Colgate-Palmolive dominates everyday essentials like toothpaste and pet nutrition, while Lululemon leads the premium athletic wear market. One offers defensive qualities in volatile markets, and the other aims for expansion in international retail. This comparison looks at their growth paths, financial health, and current valuations to help you navigate these two distinct paths.

Colgate-Palmolive reaches consumers in more than 200 countries with a diverse portfolio including oral care, home hygiene, and specialty pet nutrition. In its latest annual report, Walmart (WMT +1.51%) and its affiliates accounted for nearly 11% of total net sales. Customer concentration like this adds a layer of risk, though the company continues to expand its presence in emerging markets among consumer staples stocks.

In the 12 months ended Sept. 30, 2026, revenue reached approximately $21.3 billion, reflecting a growth rate of roughly 5.9%. Net income for the same period was close to $2.1 billion, resulting in a net margin of nearly 9.6%. These results indicate a consistent demand for hygiene and pet health products despite broader economic shifts.

As of its December 2025 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio reached approximately 158.4x, which represents the relationship between its total debt and shareholder equity. The current ratio, measuring the ability to pay short-term debts with current assets, was roughly 0.8x. In the fiscal year ended Dec. 31, 2025, free cash flow was close to $3.6 billion.

Lululemon Athletica operates a premium athletic lifestyle business focused on technical apparel, footwear, and accessories. The company uses an omni-channel approach, selling through over 800 stores and its own digital platforms. The company also uses license and supply arrangements with third parties to enter international markets like the UAE and Israel.

In the 12 months ended Aug. 2, 2026, revenue reached nearly $11.1 billion, representing a growth rate of approximately 1.7%. Net income for this period was roughly $1.4 billion, resulting in a net margin of nearly 12.8%. The slower revenue growth suggests a period of normalization following years of rapid post-pandemic expansion.

As of its February 2026 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio was nearly 0.4x, showing the company uses relatively little debt compared to its equity. The current ratio was approximately 2.3x, suggesting a strong ability to cover short-term obligations. In the fiscal year ended Feb. 1, 2026, free cash flow reached close to $921.7 million.

Colgate-Palmolive faces significant exposure to international markets and fluctuations in foreign currency values. The company deals with intense global competition from traditional rivals like Procter & Gamble (NYSE:PG) and newer private-label manufacturers. It also manages substantial legal uncertainty regarding ongoing talc-related litigation and operational risks from potential supply chain disruptions.

Lululemon Athletica manages heightened competition in the athletic apparel market, especially from imitation products. The company is vulnerable to supply chain disruptions because its manufacturing and fabric sourcing are concentrated in the APAC region. Additionally, it faces reputational risks from pending securities class action lawsuits and sensitivity to changes in U.S. tariff policy.

Lululemon Athletica appears significantly cheaper than its peer, as it carries a lower Forward P/E and a lower P/S ratio, which measures sales over the past twelve months.

Valuation metrics include sourcing from Financial Modeling Prep (FMP) and may differ from other data providers.

I'd go with Colgate-Palmolive. It sells everyday products around the world and has raised its dividend for 63 straight years, a record built on things people buy in any economy. It holds the biggest share of the world's toothpaste market, and its Hill's pet food brand adds a second source of growth.

Last quarter, sales grew in nearly every region, emerging markets like India and Brazil led the way, and management raised its profit outlook. Costs are rising and U.S. shoppers are cautious, but those pressures are hitting the whole industry, and the rest of Colgate's business is still growing.

To be fair to lululemon, it has a premium brand and $1.4 billion in cash. But sales are shrinking, with North American shoppers buying less at existing stores, and the company cut its full-year outlook in its latest report. What's more, a new CEO is still reshaping the leadership team. For investors who want to buy and hold into 2027 and beyond, Colgate offers steady growth and a dividend that gets bigger every year.

#3157. Nvidia Stock Plunge Wipes Out Nearly $500 Billion in One Day as SEC Reportedly Probes Its Accounting

A Reuters report that the SEC is looking at Nvidia's accounting sent the stock plunging on Friday. Here's what's known and what investors should do.

By Jonathan Ponciano – Nov 20, 2026 at 4:07PM EST

Shares of Nvidia (NVDA -14.01%) fell 14% on Friday afternoon, to less than $126, after Reuters reported that the Securities and Exchange Commission is investigating the chipmaker's accounting. The drop erased roughly $491 billion in market value in a single session, taking Nvidia from about $3.52 trillion to about $3.03 trillion.

Zoom out and the damage is even bigger. Nvidia closed at a record $239.24 on Oct. 6. At Friday's price, the stock is down about 48% from that high, and the company has lost about $2.7 trillion in value in just six weeks.

Here's what we know, and what investors should make of it.

The Wall Street Journal first reported on Tuesday that the SEC was investigating Nvidia but couldn't say what the probe was about. On Friday, Reuters, citing two people briefed on the matter, reported that the agency's enforcement staff are examining potential accounting issues at the company.

Many questions remain unanswered. Reuters couldn't determine when the inquiry began or which accounting practices are under review. The SEC declined to comment, and Nvidia didn't immediately respond. Keep in mind that the SEC investigates plenty of companies that are never charged with anything.

The stock was already having a bad day before the report: shares were down more than 6% earlier in the session amid a broad sell-off in AI stocks.

The probe adds to a pile of problems. Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang resigned as CEO on Nov. 11 following revelations about his personal relationships, including with a woman U.S. authorities suspect of spying for China, which China denies. The Justice Department is also reviewing Nvidia's planned $12.9 billion purchase of Hugging Face, according to Reuters.

Two areas could draw scrutiny. The first is how Nvidia reports where its sales come from. The company breaks out revenue by where customers are headquartered, rather than where they're billed. On that basis, about 63% of last quarter's revenue came from U.S.-based customers. The Financial Times has reported that Nvidia made the switch as sales billed to Singapore approached half of its total, a bad look with Southeast Asia having become a hub for chips smuggled into China.

The second is how Nvidia helps its customers pay for its chips. On Tuesday's earnings call, interim CEO Colette Kress said Nvidia's guarantees totaled $118 billion at the end of the quarter, including $105 billion of credit support tied to a single data center campus. These guarantees are the kind of disclosure the SEC is watching closely at AI companies. When a chipmaker helps fund the projects that buy its chips, it's harder to tell how much demand would exist on its own

None of this has shown up in the numbers yet. Nvidia's revenue jumped 103% to $115.8 billion last quarter, and the company expects about $130 billion this quarter. Management even raised its growth forecast for next fiscal year to about 75%. At about $126, the stock trades at roughly 12 times last quarter's adjusted earnings of $2.68 per share on an annualized basis, cheap for a company growing this fast.

But cheap can get cheaper. Accounting questions hit at the heart of what investors pay for: trust in the numbers. Until Nvidia names a permanent CEO and the SEC's focus becomes clearer, the stock could stay volatile, even after a 48% drop.

For long-term investors who already own Nvidia, there's no need to panic-sell on a report about an investigation. For anyone thinking of buying, it's smarter to wait for more clarity, or to build a position slowly, than to bet that the worst is over. There are plenty of other semiconductor stocks without a cloud of investigations hanging over them.

#3156. Your Employees’ Personal AI Agents Are Becoming Your Security Problem

David Goldschlag is co-founder and CEO of Aembit, an identity control plane for AI agents.

​Ahead of an important client meeting, a sales representative connects their personal AI agent to company email and files. The setup takes minutes and allows the employee to arrive prepared with considerably less effort, but that well-meaning shortcut may carry risks the rep never considered.

Personal AI agents, including Meta’s Muse, OpenAI’s Dots and Google’s Gemini Spark, are software assistants that can carry out routine tasks across connected services and continue working between conversations. It is early, and there is little data yet on how often employees connect these personal assistants to company accounts. But if the first numbers are any indication, the habit is forming quickly. Meta said Muse passed 10 million accounts within roughly six weeks of launch, and a Menlo Ventures survey found that 32% of U.S. adults who use AI have already let it act on their behalf without final sign-off.

For security leaders who remember the first requests to connect personal smartphones to company email, the arrival of these agentic deputies has a familiar feel. Employees found something useful and expected to use it, while IT and security were left to reconcile that enthusiasm with responsibility for company data.

Bring-your-own-device (BYOD) policies and years of “shadow IT” disputes established an enduring reality: The rank and file would have a say in the technology they used. But the analogy has limits in the AI era. Traditional software generally follows predefined workflows, while an agent can choose which tools to use and which steps to take in carrying out an employee’s request, without the employee directing each action.

Permissions granted with little consideration during setup can later support a series of actions the employee never specifically contemplated. For CISOs, the difficulty is deciding how much authority should accompany that discretion and how to enforce those limits once an AI assistant begins working.

Consider the employee preparing for the customer meeting. The request of their agent sounds innocuous: Review recent correspondence, find the relevant account documents and prepare a briefing.

Yet the permissions available during setup may cover far more information than this assignment requires. Depending on the connection, the agent may receive access to a mailbox containing correspondence with hundreds of customers, along with internal discussions unrelated to the meeting.

Suppose the employee also asks the agent to prepare and send an external follow-up. An internal document contains useful background, including an unannounced pricing change. The agent could incorporate that information into a customer message because it appears relevant to the assignment. Every connection involved might be permitted, even though the resulting disclosure was never intended. Read-only access offers limited reassurance if the agent can send what it reads through another service.

Requiring employee approval before an agent receives access provides another safeguard, but its value depends on what the employee can reasonably assess. A consent screen can describe the permissions being requested without making clear how an agent could use them together. The employee may approve those permissions without anticipating the disclosure described above.

Company policy must establish which resources an assistant may access and which actions require further review. Employees should understand their responsibilities, but connecting an agent should not leave them to determine how much authority the company is willing to delegate.

The following practices can help security leaders establish those boundaries while giving employees a practical way to use personal AI agents.

Verify that records identify which agent acted and whose authority it used. Logs that name only the employee may leave investigators unable to distinguish direct actions from those taken by an agent.

Establish which accounts and resources it can access, whether it can act in the background and how the provider handles credentials and retrieved data. Approval of an assistant should not imply approval of every connection it supports.

Where controls permit, restrict access to relevant resources and separate retrieval permissions from permission to publish or send. Enforce those limits at runtime, when the agent requests access. If a service offers only broad access, weigh that limitation in the approval decision.

Reserve employees’ attention for consequential decisions. Before an external message is sent, for example, let them review its recipients, attachments and exact content, with another review required if material details change.

Ensure security can revoke an agent’s access without disabling the employee’s account. This gives security teams a way to intervene when an agent needs to be stopped. Here, that means access revocation: withdrawing the agent’s ability to use connected systems. Cutting off access, however, does not necessarily terminate the agent’s process.

Test it against background activity and previously issued credentials, and measure how long it takes for subsequent requests to fail. Depending on the implementation, previously issued access tokens may remain usable until they expire, or a revocation decision may take time to reach every system involved. Incident procedures should account for the behavior observed in testing, including any additional steps required to contain ongoing activity.​​​

These practices also expose limitations that a policy document alone cannot resolve. If a provider cannot support sufficiently narrow access or useful audit records, the company may need to restrict the information available to that agent or decline the connection.​

The BYOD experience offers a useful lesson about AI adoption. Employees’ preferences can influence company technology decisions long before a formal policy catches up. Security leaders should take seriously the reasons people want personal agents, including the convenience of using a tool they already know.

A workable policy should give employees a clear route to request access, explain which uses are permitted and offer alternatives when a requested connection grants more authority than the business can accept. Security teams, in turn, need evidence that the agreed restrictions hold during actual use.​​​

Higher borrowing costs aren't the whole story. Here's what to consider before putting your house hunt on hold.

Mortgage rates are back up this week, wiping out modest relief from a monthlong drop that began in mid-October.

The average rate on a 30-year fixed-rate mortgage shot up 29 basis points to 7.28% APR in the week ending Nov. 19, according to rates provided to NerdWallet by Zillow. (A basis point is one one-hundredth of a percentage point.) We calculate our weekly average using daily APRs recorded over the past five business days.

A mortgage is a big ol’ loan, so when rates go up, those fractions of a percentage point add up fast. Say you’re borrowing $400,000 on a 30-year fixed-rate mortgage. Compared with last week, your monthly principal and interest payment would be about $78 higher today.

One bad week doesn't make a trend, but a jump like this can make putting your house hunt on hold until spring feel like a safer bet. So … is it?

Before deciding whether to buy a house now or wait, it helps to know what's pushing mortgage rates higher.

Right now, mortgage rates are still feeling the aftershocks from two major inflation reports last week. First, the Consumer Price Index (CPI) showed consumer prices rose more than expected in October. Then, the Producer Price Index (PPI) showed wholesale inflation climbed 6.5% over the past year — its biggest annual increase in nearly four years.

While CPI shows how prices have changed, PPI can offer clues about what's coming next. Faced with higher costs, businesses may raise their own prices to compensate, keeping inflation elevated. Federal Reserve policymakers aren't expecting much relief anytime soon, either. According to meeting minutes released Nov. 18, they expect inflation to remain elevated above their 2% target for a while.

To cool rising prices, the Fed can raise the federal funds rate, which is the benchmark interest rate banks charge each other for overnight loans. The Fed doesn't set mortgage rates, but lenders anticipate its decisions, so mortgage rates often move before the Fed acts. A rate hike is widely expected at the Fed's Dec. 8-9 meeting.

Even after a Fed rate hike, there’s no telling how quickly inflation will cool — or whether mortgage rates will follow. (Inflation is just one of many forces that affect mortgage rates, after all.) So if you do wait until spring to buy a house, don't do it just because you're betting on a cheaper mortgage.

If you're not in a rush to move, winter can be a good time to regroup. Fewer homes typically go up for sale from November through February, so waiting until spring could give you more options.

But new data from the National Association of Realtors suggests this year's slowdown goes beyond the usual seasonal lull. High mortgage rates and home prices are making it tough for many buyers to make the numbers work. For some buyers, waiting isn't a strategy — it's the only option.

Pending home sales, a measure of homes under contract, fell 16.7% in October compared with a year earlier, NAR reports. All four U.S. regions saw declines. At this rate, NAR chief economist Lawrence Yun warned that annual home sales could fall to their lowest level since the mid-1990s.

“Either sizable housing demand is building in the background, or the dream of homeownership is increasingly out of reach for many Americans,” Yun said in a news release.

Whether you're waiting by choice or necessity, you can use the time to strengthen your finances. Paying down debt, strengthening your credit score or saving for a bigger down payment could help you qualify for a better mortgage deal.

Every little bit helps when today’s mortgage rates are this high.

Mortgage preapprovals typically expire after 60 to 90 days. If you're already preapproved, why not keep an eye on listings this winter? (Hey, I’m an optimist. All it takes is one house.)

Think like a seller for a second. If you're listing your house in the dead of winter, you're probably not doing it just for fun. You might have a deadline, and you’re probably more willing to negotiate. In the winter, buyers have less competition — and more room to negotiate a lower price, closing cost credits or repairs. Those savings on the sticker price might help offset today's higher borrowing costs.

Spring typically brings more homes for sale, but it also brings more buyers competing for them. And if mortgage rates end up dropping this spring, you won't be the only one coming out of hibernation.

#3154. Marvell Reports Dec. 1. History Says What Its Stock Usually Does Next.

The chipmaker's stock has swung an average of around 12% the day after its latest reports. Which way will it go this time?

By Daniel Sparks – Nov 20, 2026 at 4:23PM EST

10 stocks we like better than Marvell Technology ›

Marvell Technology (MRVL -11.69%) will release results for its fiscal third quarter of 2027 (the period ended Oct. 31, 2026) on Tuesday, Dec. 1, with a conference call at 1:30 p.m. Pacific time.

The chipmaker's stock comes into the report at around $138 as I write, off about 56% from its June 4 record close of $316.43. And most of that drop is recent. Marvell shares ended Oct. 28 at around $252, the last trading day before speculation started about a deal for optical parts maker Lumentum Holdings.

On Nov. 2, the two companies announced an all-stock deal. After it closes, Marvell's current shareholders will own around two-thirds of the combined company. The growth stock is down about 45% from that Oct. 28 close.

The Dec. 1 report will be Marvell's first full quarterly update since it agreed to buy Lumentum. And if the past three years are any guide, the shares might make a big move the day after.

Marvell reports after the market closes, so the reaction shows up in the next day's trading. Here are its last 12 reports, the stock's close-to-close move the next day, and the revenue growth management guided for the following quarter over the quarter just reported.

Data source: Yahoo Finance and Marvell. Calculations by author.

Shares dropped the next day seven times and climbed five times.

And the moves were big either way. The average swing was around 12%, and seven of the 12 moves topped 10%.

Interestingly, the quarters themselves were almost never to blame. In all 12 reports, Marvell's revenue came in above the midpoint of its guidance.

I think the outlook mattered more. In the six reports in which management guided to next-quarter revenue growth of 6% or lower (with one guide for a decline), the stock fell the next day five times, with an average drop of around 9%.

In the six where it guided for about 8% or more, shares climbed four times, with an average gain of about 6%.

But six reports on either side doesn't prove much, and the pattern has a clear exception. In August 2026, management guided to third-quarter revenue of $3.15 billion, up 15% from the second quarter's $2.74 billion, the second-largest increase in the table. The stock still dropped 10% the next day.

A possible reason is that expectations had risen with the tech company's share price, which had more than tripled since the March 2026 report.

This time, the quarter itself could hold even less surprise than normal. When it announced the Lumentum deal on Nov. 2, Marvell said preliminary third-quarter revenue was in line with its guidance. It kept the $3.15 billion midpoint and tightened the range to plus or minus 2%.

That puts the focus on the fiscal fourth quarter, and the bar is high for a chipmaker helped by demand for artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure. Marvell's revenue climbed 22% year over year in the final quarter of fiscal 2026. Growth then rose to 28% and 37% in the first two quarters of fiscal 2027. And the $3.15 billion third-quarter midpoint means growth of around 52%, an acceleration for a third straight quarter.

"[W]e expect our revenue growth to accelerate further through the remainder of fiscal 2027," Marvell CEO Matt Murphy said in the company's fiscal second-quarter earnings release.

For growth to keep accelerating in the fiscal fourth quarter, revenue would have to exceed $3.4 billion, or about 7% above the third-quarter midpoint. In other words, a guide that just keeps pace with the third quarter might land right around the line that has split the stock's past reactions.

In the end, I'd expect a big move on Dec. 2 either way, and a down day has been a bit more common than an up day. But I wouldn't read much into one day's move when the Lumentum deal isn't expected to close until the first half of 2028.

Personally, I'd pay more attention to the size of the fourth-quarter guide than to the stock's reaction to it. Shares trade at around 20 times the earnings analysts expect for fiscal 2028, a price that seems reasonable if growth continues to accelerate. And if shares drop again on a guide that still shows accelerating growth, I think the lower price might be worth considering for investors who can ride out more swings like these.

#3152. The Next Software Revolution After AI Is Efficiency

Itamar Syn-Hershko, Founder of NeverBlink AI and BigData Boutique, helps companies confidently operate and optimize data platforms at scale.

For decades, we’ve made software easier to write, even when it meant making it more expensive to run.​

We introduced programming languages, frameworks and layers of abstraction that allowed developers to move faster. Along the way, we accepted higher memory consumption, more CPU usage and increasingly complex infrastructure.​

For the most part, this made sense. Developers were expensive, hardware kept getting cheaper and getting products to market quickly was often more important than squeezing the most out of every server.​

I think we’re approaching a point where that trade-off no longer makes sense.​

AI is changing the cost of writing software, while the growing demand for computing resources is making efficiency more important than it has been in years. Together, these forces could change not just how we build software but also the economics of the entire software industry.​

Take Java, for example. Much of its success came from making developers more productive. Automatic memory management, a rich ecosystem and portability made it easier to build and maintain complex applications without worrying about many of the details involved in lower-level programming.​

The trade-off was additional runtime overhead. Garbage collection, managed memory and abstraction layers can require considerably more resources than a carefully optimized native implementation.​

This was often a perfectly reasonable compromise. If using Java saved months of engineering work, spending a little more on servers was easy to justify.​

But what happens when AI can write, maintain and optimize complex C++ or Rust code at a fraction of the previous engineering cost?​ We should start questioning whether some of the abstractions we’ve relied on for decades are still worth their price.​

I’m not suggesting we rewrite every Java application in assembly. There are good reasons to use managed languages, including their mature tooling, ecosystems and safety characteristics. AI-generated code also introduces its own risks and still needs careful review.​

But the argument that lower-level programming is too expensive or complicated to justify is becoming much weaker.​

​At the same time, the infrastructure side of the equation is changing.​

AI is creating enormous demand for computing capacity, memory, electricity and data center space. The International Energy Agency projects that global data center electricity consumption will roughly double by 2030.​

We cannot keep solving every software performance problem by adding more hardware. At some point, the availability and cost of that hardware become serious constraints.​

There’s also growing pressure to make software cheaper.​

AI is already reducing the time and effort involved in producing software, and we should expect some of those savings to reach customers. As it becomes cheaper to build competing products, companies will find it harder to justify high prices based on development costs alone.​

This puts infrastructure efficiency at the center of the conversation. If two products offer comparable functionality but one requires a fraction of the hardware to operate, the difference can be substantial. The more efficient product can offer lower prices, better margins or both.​

​Search engines and databases are good places to look for early examples.

​Traditional search architectures (Lucene-based especially, such as Elasticsearch and OpenSearch) often require continuously provisioned compute resources and substantial memory to maintain indexes and deliver low-latency queries. This can make infrastructure costs difficult to align with fluctuating workloads.​

​Companies such as turbopuffer and WarpSearch are challenging those assumptions. Both use an object-storage-first architecture for vector and full-text search, reducing the need to keep large indexes on expensive infrastructure. A Google Cloud case study reports search and storage cost reductions of 90% for its approach.

​There are examples outside search as well, including ClickHouse, Neon, Bun and more.

​These products aren’t necessarily the result of AI-assisted development. Many of their innovations started before today’s coding agents became widely available.

​What interests me is what happens when the engineering effort required to build systems like these drops dramatically.

​For engineering leaders, this should change how we evaluate technology choices.

​We spend a lot of time measuring developer productivity, feature delivery and time to market. We should be paying just as much attention to what our software costs to operate.

​That starts with measuring actual resource consumption. Cost per query, cost per transaction, memory per workload and CPU utilization are not just infrastructure metrics. They directly affect the economics of the product.

​It also means questioning architectural decisions we’ve come to accept. Does that service really need to run continuously? Does that dataset need to stay in memory? Are we using the right algorithms and data structures? Could a more efficient implementation eliminate entire servers?

​And perhaps most importantly, we should be using AI for more than producing code faster.

​AI can help investigate performance bottlenecks, evaluate alternative algorithms, rewrite expensive components and explore lower-level implementations that would previously have required too much engineering effort.

​There are still trade-offs. Reliability, security, correctness and maintainability matter. An implementation that saves 20% in CPU costs but introduces serious operational risks is hardly an improvement.

​The point is that we now have more ways to pursue efficiency without paying the same development cost we once did.

​I expect we’ll see more companies challenge established software categories by building products that achieve similar results with much less infrastructure.

​Some will use better algorithms. Others will rethink storage architectures, eliminate unnecessary compute or replace expensive runtime components. AI will make many of these approaches easier to implement.

​For established software vendors, this creates a real challenge. Their existing architectures may have been designed around assumptions that no longer hold, while newer competitors have the freedom to start from scratch.

​For customers, it should eventually mean more capable software at lower prices.

​We’ve spent decades making software easier and cheaper to write and accepting the infrastructure overhead that came with it.

​Now that writing software is becoming cheaper, it’s time to focus on making it cheaper to run.

The recently renovated Signia by Hilton Diplomat Beach Resort offers great views, a well-equipped fitness center and delicious food.

Hilton is making a big play in South Florida with its Signia by Hilton Diplomat Beach Resort. The massive 1,000-room property — which underwent an $80 million renovation before opening under the Signia Hilton brand in May 2026 — sits on the beach in Hollywood, Florida, just outside of Fort Lauderdale.

The resort caters primarily to business and group travelers (it’s attached to a massive events space), but it’s also a strong option for vacationers looking for some R&R. The main downside: The location isn’t great if your trip primarily revolves around off-property excursions, dining and nightlife.

Room rates typically run $300 to $600 a night, depending on the season, but you can also use Hilton Honors benefits to make your stay more affordable. There’s also a resort fee of $59 per night — but Hilton waives that when you book using Hilton points.

Hilton covered the cost of my stay for two nights, but the opinions in this review are my own. Here’s what guests can expect at this oceanfront resort.

Since the Signia by Hilton Diplomat Beach Resort is part of Hilton Honors, there are several ways to book a stay there.

If you’re using Hilton points, expect to pay 70,000 to 80,000 points a night when standard rooms are available. Hilton elite status — a benefit you can earn by holding any Hilton Honors credit card — gets you the fifth-night-free perk, where you stay for at least five nights but pay for four when booking with points.

For example, if you were to stay five nights at 80,000 points a night, you’d pay 320,000 points total, bringing down your average nightly rate to 64,000 points.

You can also book using Hilton’s generous free night certificates, which can be used at almost any property in the portfolio. If you hold the Hilton Honors American Express Aspire Card, you automatically get a certificate each year. It’s also possible to earn certificates through reaching spending thresholds on the card and on the Hilton Honors American Express Surpass® Card. Terms apply.

Make sure to check the cash rate against the points rate to make sure you’re getting good value from your redemption. NerdWallet values Hilton points at 0.4 cent apiece.

For cash bookings of two nights or more, you might consider using The Hotel Collection via American Express’ travel portal for eligible cardholders. Eligible bookings come with benefits like a $100 property credit and other amenities subject to availability, including a room upgrade, early check-in and late checkout.

Keep in mind that third-party bookings typically don’t earn Hilton points or count toward elite status qualification.

It’s hard to miss the Signia by Hilton Diplomat Beach Resort, with its signature H-shaped facade and sleek white-and-glass exterior.

Stepping into the hotel, I was immediately struck by the lush greenery filling the entrance and indoor courtyard. The grand lobby has soaring glass ceilings, giving the space a greenhouse feel, although the strong air conditioning keeps you cool.

Despite its massive size, it doesn’t have a sprawling layout, which I appreciated. Everything is close together, and you can walk from the check-in counter to any of the indoor restaurants in under a minute.

I stayed in an oceanfront suite with a balcony, which was spacious and had a fun beachy vibe. To get to the rooms, you’ll need to use either the north or south tower elevator banks.

In the living room, there was a large sitting area featuring a TV, a couch, an accent chair and a four-person high-top table.

Although I didn’t spend too much time on the balcony — the October balminess was a bit too much for me — I enjoyed stepping out each morning to admire the view.

The bedroom had a king bed with extremely comfortable bedding and an oversized chair that was a great spot to relax and read a book by the window.

The bathroom was spacious, featuring a shower and a separate tub (something every room has).

Even the standard room I toured felt roomy. I liked that it shared similar elements with the suite, including the oversized lounge chair.

This is what you’d normally get when booking a room at the cheapest points price.

There are several dining venues on the property, ranging from a grab-and-go cafe to a high-end steakhouse. It is a luxury resort, so expect the prices to reflect that.

For breakfast, you can head to Palmea Kitchen, which is also open for lunch. I had the breakfast buffet, which offered a nice spread of classics, from hot food items and pastries to cold cuts and smoked salmon.

If you don’t have time for a sit-down breakfast, you can head next door to The Press, which offers made-to-order and grab-and-go food options throughout the day. You can also get smoothies, juices, snacks, pastries and other sweet treats.

The Canteen is another grab-and-go option that also sells snacks, drinks, souvenirs and sundries, similar to a convenience store.

For lunch and dinner, try Solara. It doesn’t have a traditional restaurant feel, as it’s mostly an indoor-outdoor bar space. One side connects to the lobby, while the other side faces the Solara adults-only pool.

It serves a lunch menu, as well as a substantial bar food menu that’s available late into the night.

You can also eat at Playa Beach Bar & Grill, a beachside restaurant serving Latin-inspired cuisine. I enjoyed spending a lazy lunch there and watching the waves crash onto the shore.

For a fancy sit-down dinner, go to Diplomat Prime, the property’s steakhouse. We had a group dinner at the restaurant, and the meats were, of course, the highlight. But don’t sleep on the seafood, which was also delicious.

One of the best parts of the Dip, as it’s affectionately known, is its location right on the beach. Guests can access the stretch of beach directly adjacent to the property. But it’s not a private beach, so you might encounter crowds.

I didn’t spend any time on the beach itself — it was extremely windy while I was there — but the hotel’s resort fee includes amenities like a beach lounge (umbrella not included), a daily one-hour kayak or paddleboard rental, and beachfront yoga classes.

If you don’t want to get sand everywhere, you can head to one of the three pool options: the adults-only Solara pool, the family-friendly lagoon pool and the Verandah Social Club for those 21 and older (requires paid access).

The family-friendly lagoon spans the length of the property and runs beneath the Solara pool. It also has its own hot tub.

I spent an afternoon in a cabana at the Verandah Social Club, which has some smaller plunge pools and a hot tub.

I appreciated the attentive service from the staff there, who constantly checked on whether guests needed anything.

If you’re looking for other ways to stay active, head to the two-story fitness center, featuring a variety of equipment like free weights, exercise bikes, a rowing machine and treadmills.

Next door, you’ll find the spa and wellness center. I had a relaxing massage that incorporated hot stones and aromatherapy.

The locker rooms come with a sauna and steam room, although I wished there were more amenities like a hot tub and cold plunge.

One of the resort fee inclusions is complimentary high-intensity interval training workout classes at the gym across the street. I signed up for an early morning class. The instructor was friendly, and it was a great way to start my day.

Other amenities include a complimentary one-hour e-bike rental each day, as well as a kids’ club with various activities (but drop-off fees apply).

I had a fantastic stay at this resort, but I’d recommend it for a specific traveler.

If you’re planning to stay on-property your entire trip, it’s a great option. That’s probably why it’s such a popular convention hotel, since everything you need is easily accessible.

I loved the hotel’s design, including the jungle-like atmosphere in the lobby, and I found the dining options to be tasty, albeit pricey.

But if your trip revolves around visiting Miami attractions, you’ll likely want to stay closer to the action.
